author: Akien

UNIVERSAL ADDRESSING AND BIDIRECTIONAL LINKS — napkin sketch, 2026-08-23.

The database address for a leaf is <database(per owner)>.<table>.<leaf> — short, typically shorter than file paths. All links in the database — to other database nodes and to and from files — are a tuple of 2: the local link and the remote link. File links use paths (which could include env vars).

This extends to blobs: <database(per owner)>.blobs.<rownumber>. Blob IDs are a reusable row number. Format of non-binary blobs: {LINKS: {l1 tuple, l2 tuple, ...}, WHATEVERELSE: ...} — or whatever makes sense. So when something changes address, or for deletable things, you can update everything pointing at it.

NODES are one table. TREES are always one tree per table. Anything else — blobs, embeddings, records (not a real type now but could imagine it — records held for external use, like scanned receipts, won't be deleted) — these are static lists. Void and reuse instead of delete. Only trees are really dynamic.

EMBEDDINGS ARE ANOTHER FIXED LIST. With the embedding and the metadata we have fast search, but any other search by embedding ID becomes a slow search. So instead, don't use IDs — use row number as the ID. The flaw with that is not being able to back-trace pointers to the thing being voided — but with the bidirectional link tuple, we solve it for free.

The bidirectional link tuple is load-bearing, not a convenience. It's what makes positional addressing safe for the fixed lists — when you void a row, the tuple's reverse tells you who's pointing here. Provenance is a free side effect of solving the orphan problem.

Two species in the database: TREES (dynamic, one per table, navigated by vector proximity) and LISTS (embeddings, blobs, records — static, positional, void-and-reuse). Trees link by derived similarity. Lists link by tuple. Both navigable in both directions, different reasons.

This fortifies provenance for free. And we already have most of it — this codifies it and makes it universal.
